lesson.title: Pictures that fool a model
lesson.subtitle: Tiny changes, wrong answers, and how to test for them

video.title: Pictures that fool a model
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Cards: A circle, for sure; Eight pixels changed; Now: a cross.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: My pupils trained a small model to sort drawings into circles, crosses and lines. It was sure: a circle. Then, in the lab, we changed eight pixels in just the right way, and it said cross, though the picture looked the same to us.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: pictures that fool a model, why they work, and how to test a model against them.

scenes.visual: Two columns. To us: The same picture. To the model: Tiny values pushed; A different answer.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Changed on purpose, just a little
scenes.narration: An adversarial example is an input changed on purpose, just a little, so that a model gets it wrong. People see no difference. The model reads tiny values we barely notice, and the attacker pushes exactly those.

scenes.visual: A list: Stickers on a road sign; A few changed letters; Sounds we can hardly hear.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: It's not only pictures. In tests, stickers on a road sign fooled sign readers. A few changed letters can slip a message past a filter. And sounds we can hardly hear can steer a voice assistant.

scenes.visual: Cards: Cow? Look for grass; A cow on a beach; Lost; Attackers aim at shortcuts.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Think of a pupil who learned to spot a cow by the green grass around it. Show them a cow on a beach, and they're lost. Models learn shortcuts like that too, and attackers aim at them.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Make tricky examples on purpose; Label them correctly; Train on them too; Harder to fool, not impossible.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: One defence is adversarial training: make tricky examples on purpose, label them correctly, and train on them too. The model gets harder to fool, but never impossible.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: You can test any model's answer in a similar way. Nudge the input a little, both ways, and see if the label changes. If it flips, that answer is fragile: don't let it decide alone.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A model says it's ninety-nine percent sure. Does that mean an attacker can't fool it?

scenes.visual: A list: Sure and wrong at once; 6–8 pixels flip it; Confidence is not a guarantee.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: No. A model can be sure and wrong at the same time: in the lab, a confident answer flips with six to eight pixels. Confidence is a number the model gives itself, not a guarantee.

scenes.visual: A list: Combine signals; Test with small changes; A person decides.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So where a decision matters, like a pupil's mark, a health photo or a gate that opens, don't let one model decide. Combine signals, test with small changes, and keep a person in charge.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Train it; Push pixels; It flips; Train it tough.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: fool it with a few pixels
scenes.narration: In the app, train the shapes model, then raise the pixels allowed until the right picture flips. Press “Train it tough” and attack again: fewer attacks get through.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A school plans to take attendance with a face-recognition camera, and nothing else. What's the safest plan?

scenes.visual: The summary: Tiny changes, wrong answers; Sure is not safe; Train it tough: it helps; Test it; a person decides. Takeaway: Never let one confident model decide what matters.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Tiny changes · Sure isn't safe · Train · Test
scenes.narration: Use it as a helper, with a person checking and another way in. Remember: tiny chosen changes can fool a sure model. Training it tough helps, but isn't perfect. Test with small nudges, and keep a person deciding.

scenes.visual: A list: A pupil plays the model; Smallest change that flips it; How to make it tougher?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: one pupil is the “model” and sorts drawings by a secret rule. The class hunts for the smallest change that flips its answer. Then ask: how could we make the rule harder to fool?

checkpoints.prompt: A model says it is 99% sure. Does that mean an attacker can't fool it?

options.text: No: a model can be sure and wrong at the same time
Only if it is a big model

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: confidence is a number the model gives itself, not a guarantee. A few pixels can flip a sure answer.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a model can be sure and wrong at once. In the lab, six to eight pixels flip a confident answer.

checkpoints.prompt: A school plans to take attendance with a face-recognition camera and nothing else. What is the safest plan?

options.text: Trust the camera: it's very accurate
Use it as a helper, with a person checking and another way to sign in

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: one model shouldn't decide alone. A person and a second way in catch its mistakes, honest or forced.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: an accurate model can still be fooled. Keep a person checking and another way to sign in.
